Cross-fitting, or out-of-sample residual evaluation, is a key mitigation. The task is to identify key academic literature that examines this bias. This literature should focus on residual correction, in-sample errors, and the differences in evaluation on correction-estimation and separate observations, published no later than November 2026.

The provided calculation's zero error is likely due to in-sample evaluation, failing to represent performance on unseen data. The core challenge is understanding this evaluation dependency, not quantifying a novel bias or algorithm, as this is a fundamental limitation. Key literature focuses on the optimism of in-sample error rates and cross-validation techniques. Efron's works are relevant to apparent error, covariance penalties, and cross-validation, alongside Stone's contribution to evaluating statistical predictions.

The literature review has identified several foundational works. Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman (2009) provide a comprehensive overview of training versus generalization error. Arlot and Celisse (2010) detail the inherent bias of in-sample assessment. Kriegeskorte et al. (2009) explain the pitfalls of reusing data for both selection and evaluation, leading to distorted performance metrics. Chernozhukov et al. (2018) specifically address overfitting caused by in-sample residualization.

The reviewed literature highlights the fundamental issue of data leakage when in-sample evaluation is used, leading to an overly optimistic assessment of model performance. Kapoor and Narayanan (2023) categorize this problem explicitly, while Rosset and Tibshirani (2020) mathematically distinguish between in-sample and out-of-sample error. Varma and Simon (2006) pinpoint the bias inherent in using the same data for tuning and error estimation. Xie et al. (2026) show that in-sample residual fitting does not guarantee out-of-sample error reduction.

The analysis now extends to include papers by Ye (1998) and Breiman and Spector (1992), alongside "Serving validity in adaptive data analysis," examining statistical dependencies from in-sample assessment.
